## Slide 2 · Goals for today

Three goals today. You understand how plots are created layer-wise via the
ggplot2 package. You learn how to map variables in data frames to visual aspects
of a plot. And you figure out how you can re-use code across different
visualisation tasks.

The third goal is the one that will save you the most time later, and it is the
one that surprises people: once you can make one plot, you can make most plots,
because the code barely changes.

## Slide 4 · The role of visualisation in data science

The familiar cycle, this time with the middle box in focus.

Visualisations serve at least three purposes. Exploratory data analysis: you plot
in order to understand your own data and to refine your models — these plots are
ugly and nobody else ever sees them. Communication: you plot in order to inform
others about your results, and now the plot must be readable without you standing
next to it.

And the third one, which is worth taking seriously: manipulation. Visualisations
can be used to convince others of things the data does not support — truncated
axes, misleading aggregations, cherry-picked periods. You learn this partly so
that you can recognise it when somebody tries it on you.

## Slide 5 · Why `ggplot2`

We use ggplot2, which is an easy-to-read, widely used and powerful visualisation
engine, with a large ecosystem of extensions — animated GIFs, control charts,
network plots and much more.

The property that matters pedagogically is the one in the box: the syntax is the
same for all graphs. Learning a new plot type in ggplot2 means learning one new
function name, not a new way of thinking.

## Slide 6 · What kind of plot do you want?

Before you write any code, you must decide what kind of plot you want — and that
is not a technical question.

This classic overview organises plots by what you want to show: comparison,
relationship, distribution, or composition. Start there rather than at the chart
type; the chart type follows from the question.

The important sentence: visualisation always involves prior thinking and theory.
The plot does not reveal what is in the data — it reveals what you decided to
look at.

During the session we focus on two examples: the scatter/bubble chart from
session one, and a line chart.

## Slide 7 · A very simple example to begin with

Here is a complete plot in ten lines, and every one of the ideas of this session
is already in it.

`ggplot()` takes general meta data about the plot: which data set to use, and how
variables from the data map to aesthetics of the plot. `x = gdpPercap` means "put
GDP per capita on the horizontal axis". `color = continent` means "give each
continent its own colour" — note that you never write out the colours or the
legend; both follow automatically from the variable.

Then `geom_point()` says: represent each data point by a point. And
`theme_classic()` applies a general visual theme.

Look at the plus signs at the end of the lines. That is how layers are added, and
it is the one piece of syntax that is peculiar to ggplot2.

## Slide 8 · The general idea

Every plot in ggplot2 is generated in two major steps. First you describe the
plot in all its details via a list — this is where all the work gets done. Then
you call the list and R renders the plot for you.

The practical consequence of that split is worth knowing in advance: errors
become apparent only in the second step. You can write twenty lines of perfectly
accepted description and get the error only when you print the object. So do not
be surprised when the error message points at a line that looks innocent.

You always start with an empty plot, then add layers above this empty plot, adjust
details, and that is it.

## Slide 10 · Where we want to go

Today we produce two plots: the bubble chart, which relates life expectancy to
income per capita with bubble size representing population, and a line chart
showing the divergence of income per capita over time, averaged by continent.

They look completely different. As we will see at the end, the code differs by
only a handful of lines — which is exactly the point of the session.

## Slide 11 · Developing a ggplot — the general workflow

Since we work on the graph development interactively — adding one layer at a time
and looking at the result — the slides do not reproduce every intermediate step.
The lecture notes on the course page document them for you afterwards.

The way to follow along is to add exactly one thing at a time and re-render. That
is slower than typing the whole block, and it is how you learn which line does
what.

Both data sets come ready-made from the DataScienceExercises package, so we can
concentrate on the plotting rather than on the wrangling.

## Slide 12 · The anatomy of any ggplot

This is the skeleton of every ggplot you will ever write, and it is worth
photographing.

The geom functions are the geometric forms used to represent the data: points,
lines, shades and so on. Inside them, `data` is the data to be visualised and
`mapping` is the mapping of variables in the data to the plot aesthetics — the
axes, the size, the shape, the colour.

`stat` and `position` are for more advanced cases and have sensible defaults.
Then come the coordinate function, the facet function for splitting a plot into
panels, and the theme adjustments for the look and the labels.

One practical note: data and mapping may be set as defaults within `ggplot()`, in
which case every geom inherits them, or separately for each geom, which is what
you need when you combine several data sets in one figure.

## Slide 13 · From the bubble to the line chart

Here are the two plots side by side as code, and this slide is the punchline of
the session.

What changed? The data set, from one year of countries to continent averages over
time. The mappings: `size` disappears, `fill` becomes `color`, and the x axis
becomes the year. One new geom is added, `geom_line()`, because we now want lines
between the points. The size scale is no longer required. The number formatting
moves from the x axis to the y axis. And the labels are adjusted.

Everything else is identical. Two visually completely different figures, and
perhaps eight lines of real difference.

Two details worth noting. `shape = 21` in the bubble chart is the point shape
that has both a fill and a border, which is why it uses `fill` rather than
`color`. And `alpha = 0.65` makes the bubbles semi-transparent, so that
overlapping bubbles remain readable — indispensable for this kind of chart.

## Slide 14 · Summary

To summarise: visualisations serve many purposes, including the exploration of
your data and the communication of your results. We learned how to visualise data
stored in data frames via ggplot2. And while there are many different plot
variants, their syntax is very similar.

Code for different plots differs mainly by the aesthetic mappings and the geoms
used, which allows you to re-use a lot of code. In practice you will keep a file
of plots you once made and start from the closest one.

## Slide 15 · How to get better

A great way to learn how to plot is to replicate examples from the internet and
adjust them to your own data. Two resources are particularly good: "From Data to
Viz", which helps you choose the plot type and then links to the code, and the R
Graph Gallery, which has hundreds of worked examples.

And the same caveat as in the import session applies to AI here: once you
understand the basic functioning, AI can be a very effective assistant for
creating visualisations. It is good at the tedious parts — legend positioning,
axis formatting, colour scales. It cannot tell you whether the plot answers your
question, and it will happily produce a beautiful chart of the wrong thing.
